generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA), such as a BCC MoNbTaW alloy, exhibits strongly temperature‐dependent plastic deformation behavior because the relative ease of thermally activated dislocation movement changes with temperature. At lower temperatures, plasticity is primarily accommodated by thermally limited double‐kink nucleation of screw dislocations, whereas at elevated temperatures, enhanced edge dislocation mobility (and possibly minor twinning or phase transformation) leads to a pronounced softening and increased ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline, undeformed refractory high‐entropy alloy in its BCC phase (e.g., MoNbTaW) with a distorted lattice from multiple principal elements.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to in situ high‐temperature mechanical testing over a temperature range from room temperature to elevated temperatures while monitoring deformation.
generation.conditions: Controlled tensile or compression testing under a temperature ramp, combined with in situ structural characterization (e.g., TEM, high‐energy XRD) and supported by atomistic/mesoscale simulations.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure’s dislocation configuration, specifically the activation and mobility of screw versus edge dislocations, along with possible minor phase transitions or twinning.
generation.mechanism: Temperature variation changes the activation energy barriers for dislocation motion. At lower temperatures, plastic deformation is dominated by thermally limited double‐kink nucleation of screw dislocations. As temperature increases, edge dislocations become more mobile and may activate additional deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning), resulting in a transition to a more ductile response.
generation.predicted_outcome: With increasing temperature, a shift in the dominant plastic deformation mechanism will be observed—from a regime governed by screw dislocation motion with high yield stress at room temperature to one where enhanced edge dislocation mobility lowers the yield strength and increases ductility. Macro-scale measurements should reveal increased plastic strain rates and reduced yield strength at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Room temperature mechanical testing data showing higher yield strength and dislocation behaviors dominated by screw dislocation double‐kink processes.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected within a temperature range that enhances dislocation mobility without inducing excessive grain boundary sliding or dramatic microstructural degradation. Beyond a certain high temperature, other softening mechanisms or instability effects may override the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature thresholds for the transition between dislocation mechanisms and the quantitative changes in yield stress and ductility are not precisely known and require further combined experimental and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature tensile or compression tests on polycrystalline MoNbTaW samples while concurrently imaging dislocation behavior using TEM or high-energy XRD. Parallel atomistic/mesoscale simulations under the same conditions would predict dislocation behavior as a function of temperature.
measurements: Yield stress and ductility as a function of temperature
Dislocation density and type (screw vs. edge) via microstructural imaging
Slip behavior and strain rate localization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dominant dislocation mechanism does not shift with temperature—i.e., if dislocation analysis shows no significant increase in edge dislocation mobility or related deformation mechanisms at higher temperatures, or if the plastic deformation response (yield strength reduction and ductility increase) does not correlate with temperature as predicted—the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are designed for high elevated-temperature strength, with both edge and screw dislocations playing an important role for plastic deformation. However, they can also display a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering (SRO). Here, we investigate mechanisms underlying the mobilities of screw and edge dislocations in the body-centered cubic MoNbTaW RHEA over a wide temperature range using extensive molecular dynamics simulations based on a highly-accurate machine-learning interatomic potential. Further, we specifically evaluate how these mechanisms are affected by the presence of SRO. The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced, although this influence of SRO appears to be attenuated at increasing temperature. Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
